system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2155-02-22 16:24:00 to 2155-03-03 15:42:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis due to a CFTR gene mutation, depression, anxiety, seizure disorder, and a history of venous thrombosis, was admitted for an acute exacerbation characterized by epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She was managed with IV fluids, Dilaudid for pain, and antiemetics per protocol. A PICC line was placed on hospital day 4 to ensure reliable venous access. Her diet was advanced as tolerated, and home medications, including Lamictal, were restarted. During the stay, a prolonged QT interval was noted, prompting discontinuation of Seroquel and promethazine. She was treated for mild otitis externa with ear drops. The patient improved clinically and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to hold Seroquel until cardiac evaluation, follow up with her primary care provider, and continue all other medications.
problems: Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified
Migraine, unspecified, not intractable, without status migrainosus
Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus
Personal history of other venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with chronic pancreatitis requiring IVF/IV
medications, poor PIV access, previously requiring ___ guided PICC placement in
past admissions  // place PICC

COMPARISON:
Study from ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiologist performed the
procedure. agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.
.

PROCEDURE:
1. Single lumen mid line placement through the brachial vein on the right.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the brachia
vein on the right was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained before and after
intravenous access, which confirmed vein patency.  Venogram was performed.  A
peel-away sheath was then placed over a guidewire. The guidewire was then
advanced into the proximal brachial vein using fluoroscopic guidance. 
Attempts to advance the guidewire centrally were unsuccessful.  A single lumen
mid line measuring 10 cm in length was then placed through the peel-away
sheath with its tip positioned in the proximal brachial vein under
fluoroscopic guidance. Position of the catheter was confirmed by a
fluoroscopic spot film of the arm. The peel-away sheath and guidewire were
then removed. The catheter was secured to the skin, flushed, and a sterile
dressing applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  The accessed right brachial vein was patent and compressible.
2.  Venogram showing stenosis of the proximal brachial / axillary vein with
reconstitution of flow through venous collaterals.
2.  Brachialvein approach single lumen right midline with tip in the proximal
right brachial vein.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a right 10 cm brachial approach single lumen midline
with tip in the proximal brachial vein.  The line is ready to use.

TECHNIQUE:  Single phase split bolus contrast: MDCT axial images were acquired
through the abdomen and pelvis following intravenous contrast administration
with split bolus technique.
Oral contrast was not administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.

DOSE:  Acquisition sequence:
   1) Stationary Acquisition 5.5 s, 0.5 cm; CTDIvol = 26.5 mGy (Body) DLP =
13.2 mGy-cm.

mGy-cm.
 Total DLP (Body) = 681 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen pelvis dated ___

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: There is bibasilar atelectasis.  There is no pleural or
pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates homogenous attenuation throughout. 
There is no evidence of focal lesions.  There is no evidence of intrahepatic
or extrahepatic biliary dilatation.  The gallbladder is surgically absent.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding.

SPLEEN: The spleen shows normal size and attenuation throughout, without
evidence of focal lesions.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram. 
There is no evidence of focal renal lesions or hydronephrosis.  There is no
perinephric abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach is unremarkable.  Small bowel loops demonstrate
normal caliber, wall thickness, and enhancement throughout.  Evaluation of the
colon is somewhat limited as it is largely decompressed however there is a

a similar distribution to the prior CT.  The appendix is normal.

PELVIS: The urinary bladder and distal ureters are unremarkable.  There is no

REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: The uterus is of normal size and enhancement. There is no

LYMPH NODES: There is no retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  There
is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

VASCULAR: There is no abdominal aortic aneurysm.  No atherosclerotic disease
is noted.

BONES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or acute fracture. 
Chronic mild compression deformity of T12 is unchanged.

SOFT TISSUES:  There is stranding of the soft tissues overlying the right hip.

IMPRESSION:


1. No evidence of bowel obstruction, pseudocyst, or pancreatic mass.
2. Featureless appearance of the colon from the splenic flexure to the rectum

3. Stranding in the soft tissues overlying the right hip could be related to

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me about what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve had this pain in my upper belly for two days now. It’s the same kind I get with my pancreatitis—fullness, radiating to my back. I’ve been nauseous and throwing up, haven’t kept anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, cough, or urinary symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or anything like that. Just the pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We know you have chronic pancreatitis from your CF gene mutation, and you usually don’t have high lipase during flares. We’ll treat this as an acute flare. We’ve started IV fluids and Dilaudid for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That last dose already helped a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs. Your lipase is 50, which is normal, but that fits your history. Liver enzymes are a bit high, but not alarming. We’ll keep you NPO for now and give nutrition through the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I usually can’t eat during these flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but better than yesterday. Still nauseous though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the IV anti-nausea meds going. Also, you mentioned a headache—any idea what kind it is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feels like my usual migraines. I’ve taken Fioricet before, even when I’m NPO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll give you Fioricet every four hours as needed. We’ll also keep monitoring your heart with EKGs since you’re on Seroquel and amitriptyline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, is that because of the long QT issue last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your QTc was 440 on admission—within normal, but we’re cautious. We’ll recheck it after restarting your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids today if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’d love to try something small.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow. Also, we’re restarting your home meds—Lisinopril, amlodipine, omeprazole, and Lamictal—since you’re tolerating PO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Seroquel and amitriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart those today too, but we’ll monitor your EKG closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re switching from IV Dilaudid to your oral tramadol for pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I prefer the tramadol anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, we noticed a sore on your lower gum. Is that from biting it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I must’ve bitten it when I was dry heaving. It’s pretty painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you lidocaine viscous mouthwash to use before meals to help with the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ordering a CT scan today to make sure there’s no pseudocyst or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Last time it was clear, so I hope this is too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT came back. No pseudocyst, no obstruction, no mass. Your pancreas looks normal. The colon has some changes from old colitis, but nothing new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s just the flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re confident it’s acute on chronic pancreatitis. We’ll keep advancing your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a midline in your right arm today. Your veins have been tough to access, and this will help with fluids and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar, but shorter and doesn’t go as far. It’s safer given your history of clots in the left arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The midline was placed successfully in your right brachial vein. It’s working well, and you’re already getting fluids through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I hope this helps avoid more needle sticks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been reviewing your labs. Your hemoglobin is low at 9.1, but it’s stable for you. It’s normocytic, and iron studies are normal, so it’s likely chronic underproduction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no transfusion needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. It’s not causing symptoms, and you’re not actively bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your EKG today shows QTc of 449. It’s slightly up from admission, but still not prolonged. We’ll follow up with your PCP to check it again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop Seroquel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll keep it for now. But your PCP will need to check your heart function and possibly do an echo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re eating regular food, pain is controlled with oral meds, and you’re moving around fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll discharge you on your regular meds, including tramadol, Creon, and your psychiatric medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the mouth sore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using the lidocaine rinse. See your dentist or PCP if it doesn’t heal in a week or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the weight check you mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, weigh yourself daily. If you gain more than three pounds, call your doctor—could be fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting with your right arm for a few days because of the midline. Otherwise, resume normal activities as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What’s the plan after discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications as prescribed. Follow up with your PCP in a week, especially for the EKG to check your QTc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain specialist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with Dr. ___ for pain management. Same for your psychiatrist and neurologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been through a lot, but I feel much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. We’re confident you’ll continue to improve at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call us if symptoms return or if you have any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge papers are ready. You’ll get prescriptions for all your meds, including Creon and tramadol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll make sure to pick them up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep using the lidocaine rinse for the mouth ulcer until it heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Any diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low-fat diet as usual. Small, frequent meals. Avoid alcohol completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know the drill. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the discharge team get you ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your midline will be removed at your follow-up if it’s no longer needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll let them know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep monitoring your weight and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my triggers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Stay in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. The nurse will assist you with discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis due to a CFTR gene mutation, cardiomyopathy, depression, anxiety, seizure disorder, and a history of venous thrombosis, was admitted for an acute exacerbation characterized by epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She was managed with IV fluids, IV Dilaudid for pain, and antiemetics per protocol. A midline catheter was placed on hospital day 6 to ensure reliable venous access. Her diet was advanced as tolerated, and home medications, including Lamictal, Seroquel, and amitriptyline, were restarted once she could tolerate oral intake. She was treated for migraine headaches with Fioricet and for an aphthous ulcer with lidocaine viscous mouthwash. A CT scan showed no pseudocyst, obstruction, or mass. Her QTc interval was monitored due to psychiatric medications and remained within acceptable limits. The patient improved clinically and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with her PCP for EKG monitoring, continue all medications, and monitor her weight for fluid retention.
